definition.text: Gretchen Daily (born 1964) is an American environmental scientist and tropical ecologist who advanced the science of ecosystem services and ways to value nature in decisions.

facts.text: She edited Nature's Services: Societal Dependence on Natural Ecosystems (1997), a foundational framework for understanding nature's benefits to people.
Nature's Services served as a model for ecosystem regulation in several regions and was a catalyst for the UN's Millennium Ecosystem Assessment.
Her original definition kept ecosystem goods and ecosystem services apart, a distinction later work lumped together.
In 2005 she co-founded the Natural Capital Project with The Nature Conservancy and World Wildlife Fund to bring nature's values into decision-making.
The Project's open-source software InVEST is used in 185 countries to show nature's values in specific decisions.
Her 2002 book with Katherine Ellison, The New Economy of Nature, gives cases where companies or governments profited from conservation.

definition.text: Allen V. Kneese (1930–2001) was an American economist and a pioneer of environmental economics.

facts.text: His research built pollution into economic models and studied economic incentives for environmental improvement.
He was the first president of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists and a founding editor of the Journal of Environmental Economics and Management.
He worked at Resources for the Future from 1961, and shared the first Volvo Environment Prize with John V. Krutilla in 1990.

definition.text: AnnMari Jansson (1934–2007) was a Swedish systems ecologist who helped pioneer research joining ecology and economics.

facts.text: In 1982, with economist Karl-Göran Mäler, she gathered ecologists and economists at a Saltsjöbaden symposium on integrating ecology and economy.
She helped found the International Society for Ecological Economics in 1988 and edited its journal Ecological Economics from 1989.
Her ecological work drew on the models of Howard T. Odum.

definition.text: C. S. 'Buzz' Holling (1930–2019) was a Canadian ecologist and one of the conceptual founders of ecological economics.

facts.text: He introduced ideas including resilience, adaptive management, the adaptive cycle and panarchy.
His 1973 paper on the resilience of ecological systems had a large impact across natural and social sciences.
In his usage, resilience is an ecosystem's resistance to shifting into another state.
He was among the first ecologists to recognise the importance of nonlinear dynamics.
He founded the Resilience Alliance and the journal Conservation Ecology, now Ecology and Society.

definition.text: David Pearce (1941–2005) was a British pioneer of environmental economics and professor at University College London.

facts.text: He set out techniques for valuing nature, arguing that the environment is under-priced and that the benefits of environmental services can be calculated.
His early work on cost-benefit analysis, pollution and resource depletion came before these ideas reached mainstream economics and policy.
He advised UK ministers and was a convening lead author for the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.
He criticised the assumptions behind discounting future goods.
